answer.rationale: The finance mandate of an 18% component spend cut cannot be met by the incumbent, who has already refused to reopen price this cycle. The low-cost vendor's quote meets the mandate standalone. Memory c2 provides prior-cycle evidence that the switch is operationally sound: unit cost fell sharply, onboarding was quick, and invoicing remained accurate—no hidden cost of ownership surfaced in that prior year of use. Memory c6 shows that the incumbent's multi-year volume pricing, while attractive, was predicated on a longer-term commitment that locks in scope and cost; with the incumbent refusing renegotiation and the 14-day expiry hard, that path is now closed anyway. I will verify c2 to confirm the onboarding and invoicing details still hold under the current contract window, and verify c1 to confirm what integration stability would be forgone by not renewing—so I can plan a fallback if the low-cost vendor underperforms. I will not pull a second-source contract simultaneously; the primary objective is cost, and the assembly line at 94% with no buffer means I cannot afford two onboarding disruptions. If the switch clears a short guarded test (e.g., first two delivery windows), I will revisit second-sourcing in the next review cycle. The 14-day clock and the non-auto-renew clause make defer_decision untenable; negotiate_terms is exhausted by the incumbent's refusal; adding a second source does not by itself meet the 18% cut this cycle.
